name: Amurdak
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Handelsmann, R. 1991. Towards a description of Amurdak: a language of northern Australia. Honours thesis, University of Melbourne
earlier_scan.note: unpublished thesis not online; Mailhammer's published Amurdak work (2009 AJL) is morphosyntax

new_statements.quote: I have as yet been unable to isolate the precise combination of pitch, intensity and length which constitutes stress or prominance in Amurdak. What I occasionally perceive as a stressed syllable in one instantiation of a word, I often perceive as not stressed in another instantiation of the same word. This is common in Iwaidja. Pym & Larrimore (1979) include a chapter on 'discourse phonology' in their description of Iwaidja, devoted to the question of why word stress appeared to vary. [...] I have been unsuccessful in getting native speakers' intuitions in this area.
new_statements.citation: Handelsmann, Robert. 1991. Towards a description of Amurdak: a language of Northern Australia. Honours thesis, Department of Linguistics & Language Studies, University of Melbourne (submitted November 1991). vii + 116 pp.
new_statements.locator: §2.3 Stress, p. 38 (PDF page 47 of the ANU scan; page image page_pins/)
new_statements.rule_in_words: The only first-hand description declines to give a placement rule: the author could not identify a consistent phonetic correlate of stress, and the syllable heard as prominent shifts from one token of a word to another; he likens this to Iwaidja, where Pym & Larrimore (1979: 11) found syllable grouping mattered more for intelligibility than stress placement. No fixed, weight-based or lexical rule is stated or implied.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the section is a statement of indeterminacy rather than a rule. Elsewhere the thesis mentions speakers' slow syllabifications sometimes breaking words into 'groups of syllables' whose status (morphological or metrical) is unclear (p. 12, fn. 6), and occasional compensatory vowel lengthening before simplified clusters (§2.6, p. 45) — neither is tied to stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, elicited citation forms and repeated tokens of single words from two speakers (Big Bill Neidjie and Nelson Mulurinj), fieldwork 1990-91; no discourse-level analysis was done for Amurdak.
new_statements.identity_note: Handelsmann 1991 describes the Amurdak of two speakers, Big Bill Neidjie and Nelson Mulurinj, recorded around Oenpelli / Mt Borradaile (East Alligator area) in 1990-91; the thesis names no dialect (Wikipedia lists Urrirk and Gidjurra as dialects; glottocode amar1271 is language-level). Capell 1942 calls the language 'Amarag' (also 'Umoriu' after Spencer) — same language, single Oenpelli speaker. No differently-named variety is at issue.

sources.note: Ch. 2 Phonology has a dedicated §2.3 Stress (p. 38): the author could not isolate the combination of pitch, intensity and length that constitutes stress in Amurdak; a syllable perceived as stressed in one token of a word is perceived as unstressed in another token of the same word ('This is common in Iwaidja', citing Pym & Larrimore 1979 discourse phonology, p. 11); no native-speaker intuitions obtained. No placement rule given anywhere in the thesis (only other 'stress' hits are a quotation about Gagudju /l/ allophony, p. 10, and bibliography entries).
Consonant and vowel tables attributed to Mailhammer 2009 and Evans 1998; nothing on stress. Lists Handelsmann 1991, Mailhammer 2009, Neidjie et al. 2009 Amurdak inyman, Evans 1998.

sources.note: Amarag section gives free pronouns, possessives, verb prefixing and object clitics from one Oenpelli speaker via Gunwinggu; says only 'phonetically it is simpler than some'. No stress or accent statement for Amarag (the only accent remark in the article is for Margu, sec. 24).
Bare wordlist in phonetic transcription; no stress marks, no statement.
